newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German EMU debate clouded by targets-Krupp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German EMU debate clouded by targets-Krupp.

text.p: Public debate in Germany on the European single currency has become obsessed with economic targets, neglecting the overall picture as countries progress towards the planned 1999 start date, a Bundesbank council member said on Thursday.

Hans-Juergen Krupp said the discussion over European economic and monetary union (EMU) in Germany was missing the point -- failing to see that the Maastricht Treaty calls for sustained convergence and does not pinpoint specific targets.

"Media and public opinion in Germany are fixated on adhering to the two reference levels for the budget criterion, although the Treaty expressly allows for exceptions and demands an assessment of the overall situation," Krupp said.
"I regret that in Germany there is not a debate about the necessity for consolidation, but about meeting the reference levels which according to the Treaty do not have to be met."
Krupp was speaking at the annual conference of the state central bank of Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and Schleswig-Holstein, of which he is president.

While the German government has pledged to bring its budget deficit down to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, many analysts say this is over-ambitious and say the level is more likely to be around 3.2 to 3.4 percent.

Quibbling about the Maastricht Treaty's deficit goals, which states a nation's deficit should be no more than three percent of gross domestic product, has become the hot topic as Germany's high unemployment level and sluggish econmic growth cast a question mark over whether it can qualify for EMU.
But many also say that Germany's stable economic history, combined with allowances made for the cost of reunification in 1990, will push the country though the Maastricht goal.
Krupp applauded what he termed "impressive progress" among European Union nations seeking to achieve economic convergence for the single currency,

Referring to European Commission forecasts released on Wednesday which predicted all EU states would meet EMU criteria except Italy and Greece, Krupp said: "If five years ago one had predicted Italy would reach that level, one would not have been believed. Progress on convergence in Europe has been impressive."
The EC said Italy's deficit to GDP ratio would hit 3.2 percent this year.
Turning to the domestic economy, Krupp said that Germany would be making a risky move if it decided to cut its interest rates in present circumstances.

While the German economy was free from any inflationary threat, he said any easing of credit rates could affect foreign exchange movements, thereby possibly boosting import prices and unemployment, and may lead to higher bond yields.
"Interest rate cuts at the moment would entail considerable risks," he said. "One would have to keep checking whether the expected advantages are sufficiently great to warrant taking the risks."
The Bundesbank has kept its key 2.50 percent discount and 4.50 Lombard rates on hold since April 1996, while the repo rate has been kept at three percent since August last year.
Noting the recent sharp decline in the mark against the dollar, Krupp said this should be seen as a normalisation phase rather than a depreciation.

He said the mark's weakness did not warrant concern about price pressure at the moment, but asked whether the decline had been weathered without inflation risks, he added: "That depends how the economy develops. It is hard to assess."
The federal statistics office said earlier that annual consumer price inflation at 1.4 percent in April, well inside the Bundesbank's traditional 2.0 percent desirable level.
